title: A loader learns to balance
lead: ETH Zurich and partners taught a loader to balance and travel on its front wheels. Controllers learned in simulation before being tested on the physical hydraulic machine.

news.title: A five-tonne loader learns to balance on two wheels
news.summary: ETH Zurich and partners trained hydraulic-loader controllers in simulation and transferred them to a physical machine. A John Deere 332G balanced on its front wheels, moved while balancing and returned to four-wheel support.
news.details: Researchers from ETH Zurich, Blue River Technology, Gravis Robotics and Intel trained a five-tonne John Deere 332G loader to perform dynamic maneuvers autonomously. The work appeared in Science Robotics on November 11, with an author manuscript posted to arXiv on November 13. Controllers learned in simulation and were then deployed on the actual machine. It could swing onto its front wheels, maintain balance while moving and articulating the bucket, and return to four wheels.
news.technical_novelty: ETH Zurich and partners trained hydraulic-loader controllers in simulation and transferred them to a physical machine. A John Deere 332G balanced on its front wheels, moved while balancing and returned to four-wheel support. Hydraulic actuation makes this demanding: fluids, flexible components and delays create a nonlinear relationship between commands and movement. Reinforcement learning improves a controller according to the results of attempted behavior. The authors divided the maneuver into swing-up, stabilization, velocity tracking and soft landing. They varied simulated conditions so training would not depend on one exact set of machine parameters. A separate simulated swing-up evaluation covered one thousand randomized environments. The evaluation examined final pitch before switching to the stabilizing controller, tying its success criterion to the transition between two behaviors.
news.engineering_impact: ETH Zurich and partners trained hydraulic-loader controllers in simulation and transferred them to a physical machine. A John Deere 332G balanced on its front wheels, moved while balancing and returned to four-wheel support. Balancing a heavy machine looks like one trick, but the study divides it into connected problems. It must build the necessary body motion, hold its pitch, follow a velocity command and lower its wheels gently. Simulation lets the team repeatedly vary those attempts without exposing the physical loader to every failed version. The trained programs were then tested on the machine itself. That physical step connects learning in a virtual environment with the response of hydraulics and a heavy chassis in the experiment.
news.limitations: ETH Zurich and partners trained hydraulic-loader controllers in simulation and transferred them to a physical machine. A John Deere 332G balanced on its front wheels, moved while balancing and returned to four-wheel support. The study documents additional command filtering during balanced travel. This shows how the way commands are applied remains a practical part of operating the physical machine.
news.evidence_status: Research combining simulation training and physical-loader demonstrations; published in Science Robotics on November 11.
news.organization: ETH Zurich; Blue River Technology; Gravis Robotics; Intel

news.title: Simulation training teaches a reasoning model to operate a robot
news.summary: An MIT-led team trained an open-weight reasoning model to choose robot-arm movements using simulated trials alone. On a real dual-arm robot, the trained model completed 60% of 30 trials, while the starting model completed none.
news.details: Researchers from MIT, UC Berkeley, UC San Diego, NVIDIA and Inco AI presented simulation-based robot training for a reasoning model on November 13. Qwen3.8-27B, a model with 27 billion learned parameters, receives images, arm state and an instruction, works through intermediate reasoning steps and selects the tool's next pose. Inverse kinematics converts that target into a joint configuration executed by the arm controller. The reported additional training did not use demonstrations of the desired actions.
news.technical_novelty: An MIT-led team trained an open-weight reasoning model to choose robot-arm movements using simulated trials alone. On a real dual-arm robot, the trained model completed 60% of 30 trials, while the starting model completed none. The team built PEAR, a software engine for training through robot trials, and used the LIBERO and RoboDojo simulated task environments. Reinforcement learning adjusts behavior according to the outcome of attempts. LIBERO success rose from 1.6% to 74.4%. For physical transfer, each model received 30 trials on a dual-arm robot, covering lifting different objects by ten centimeters and aligning three blocks using a set square. The trained model succeeded in 60%, versus none for the base model. Trials had a limit of 25 observation-and-action rounds; retrying an invalid action also consumed a round.
news.engineering_impact: An MIT-led team trained an open-weight reasoning model to choose robot-arm movements using simulated trials alone. On a real dual-arm robot, the trained model completed 60% of 30 trials, while the starting model completed none. The robot is taught through the outcome of simulated attempts rather than recordings of the right motion. The model observes a scene, proposes the next pose, receives another observation and continues. The same sequence is used on the physical arm, allowing a test of whether a useful problem-solving behavior transfers. The 60% result needs its thirty-trial context: specified object lifts and block alignment, with limits on action rounds and reasoning length. Those details explain what the reported success actually measures.
news.limitations: An MIT-led team trained an open-weight reasoning model to choose robot-arm movements using simulated trials alone. On a real dual-arm robot, the trained model completed 60% of 30 trials, while the starting model completed none. Further RoboDojo training stopped after two tasks because of computing resources. The authors explicitly identify the limited variety of simulators and training tasks as a current restriction.
news.evidence_status: Author preprint with simulated evaluation and 30 physical trials per model; no independent replication is established here.
news.organization: MIT; UC Berkeley; UC San Diego; NVIDIA; Inco AI

news.title: NTT West and Iris Ohyama connect building cameras with robots
news.summary: Iris Ohyama and NTT West tested camera-to-cleaner instructions and coordination between different robot types. The companies report technical feasibility for a chain linking image interpretation with machine action.
news.details: Iris Ohyama and communications company NTT West reported a second stage of facility-and-robot integration trials on November 16. Images from a security camera were analyzed and the resulting information used to instruct the JILBY cleaning robot. Another example linked that machine with the ugo Nova humanoid, sharing information and allocating tasks according to their respective capabilities. The announcement describes verification that the connections could work technically, without specifying trial counts or completed-job rates.
news.technical_novelty: Iris Ohyama and NTT West tested camera-to-cleaner instructions and coordination between different robot types. The companies report technical feasibility for a chain linking image interpretation with machine action. NTT West develops the shared management system, called the Multi-Robotics Platform. It consolidates equipment information on remote servers. In its architecture, a vision-language model interprets the surroundings; a large language model generates instructions. A vision-language-action model supports choosing actions from images and instructions. These are the roles referred to as VLM, LLM and VLA. An earlier stage connected human communication and cleaning-data analysis with suggestions for routes, cleaning frequency and timing. The newly described work connects facility observations with coordination across different machines.
news.engineering_impact: Iris Ohyama and NTT West tested camera-to-cleaner instructions and coordination between different robot types. The companies report technical feasibility for a chain linking image interpretation with machine action. Different machines in a building can use information from one observation while performing different actions. Here the camera is part of the facility, and its image becomes an input to shared management. Language-based models connect a situation description to a task, while the action model supports execution. Robotics therefore involves relationships among several devices as well as the behavior of one machine. To judge how reliably those relationships work, error measurements at the connections would be useful; the authors currently report that the architecture functioned.
news.limitations: Iris Ohyama and NTT West tested camera-to-cleaner instructions and coordination between different robot types. The companies report technical feasibility for a chain linking image interpretation with machine action. A camera-and-cleaner demonstration is planned at Tokyo Big Sight on November 18–20. These are research demonstrations, and the particular examples differ between exhibition venues.
news.evidence_status: The partners' report of technical feasibility; quantitative reliability measurements are not published.

news.title: ROBOTERA aligns a robot hand with human demonstration hardware
news.summary: ROBOTERA opened orders for its five-finger XHAND 1 Pro-U robot hand. Matching its joints to the wearable DexUMI recorder supports transferring human demonstrations to a two-arm robot.
news.details: ROBOTERA announced the commercial release of XHAND 1 Pro-U on November 16. The five-finger hand has 16 degrees of freedom, meaning independent directions in which its joints can change configuration. Its mechanism closely matches DexUMI, a wearable hand exoskeleton from NVIDIA GEAR Lab that records human demonstrations. Corresponding joints make it easier to map demonstrated motion to the robot. The redesign also changes thumb placement, hand articulation and tactile sensing on the palm side.
news.technical_novelty: ROBOTERA opened orders for its five-finger XHAND 1 Pro-U robot hand. Matching its joints to the wearable DexUMI recorder supports transferring human demonstrations to a two-arm robot. A person wearing the exoskeleton handles real objects while the recorder collects hand movement and fingertip force information. Those demonstrations are used for additional training of the GR00T 2 robot-control model, after which a dual-arm robot uses two matching hands. The release describes three multi-step evaluations: banana-yogurt preparation, granola scooping and a match-and-lamp chemistry task. Reported overall success rates are respectively 60%, 80% and 75%. For the tasks shown, the company says training used DexUMI demonstrations without extra task-specific recordings made by remotely controlling the target robot or additional robot-practice data.
news.engineering_impact: ROBOTERA opened orders for its five-finger XHAND 1 Pro-U robot hand. Matching its joints to the wearable DexUMI recorder supports transferring human demonstrations to a two-arm robot. A human example contains both finger motion and contact force. Corresponding joints make it easier to preserve the relationship between a gesture and the receiving hand's mechanics. In the reported workflow, a model learns from those records and then carries out a complete sequence with two robot arms. A useful question for each success percentage is which task it measures. Here there is a separate result for each of three sequences.
news.limitations: ROBOTERA opened orders for its five-finger XHAND 1 Pro-U robot hand. Matching its joints to the wearable DexUMI recorder supports transferring human demonstrations to a two-arm robot. ROBOTERA opened commercial orders for the first 40 hands. The described results concern the specific exoskeleton, model and two-arm configuration; trial counts for the percentages are not stated.
news.evidence_status: Manufacturer-reported results for three multi-step tasks; trial counts are not stated in the release.

news.title: Robot-safety supplier FORT discloses growth ahead of a proposed listing
news.summary: FORT Robotics reported $12.5 million in revenue for the first nine months of 2026, up 52.5% year over year. Its proposed combination with Newbury Street II also brings disclosures about the installed base for robot-safety infrastructure.
news.details: FORT Robotics, a supplier of safety systems for robotic machines, published financial and operating information on November 16 as it prepares a proposed combination with Newbury Street II. Revenue for the nine months ended September 30 reached $12.5 million, an increase of 52.5% from the corresponding period a year earlier. Gross margin, the share of revenue remaining after cost of sales, rose to 67.6% from 66.6%. The figures concern a business supplying protective infrastructure to robot developers and users.
news.technical_novelty: FORT Robotics reported $12.5 million in revenue for the first nine months of 2026, up 52.5% year over year. Its proposed combination with Newbury Street II also brings disclosures about the installed base for robot-safety infrastructure. FORT says its products are deployed across more than 23,000 units for over 680 customers. Named customers include Agility Robotics, DoorDash, Cobot, Zoox and Google DeepMind. The companies publicly filed a Form S-4, a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission registration statement for the proposed combination, on November 13. The November 16 release says it has not yet become effective. Closing is expected in the fourth quarter of 2026 or first quarter of 2027, conditional on the stated approvals and other requirements.
news.engineering_impact: FORT Robotics reported $12.5 million in revenue for the first nine months of 2026, up 52.5% year over year. Its proposed combination with Newbury Street II also brings disclosures about the installed base for robot-safety infrastructure. Robots are surrounded by a market for hardware and software supporting work alongside people. FORT sells that protective infrastructure to multiple developers and users. Its revenue announcement therefore describes a different part of the industry from the release of a control model. It plans to become publicly traded through combination with a company established to acquire a business. Financial disclosure makes it possible to follow the scale of this supplier and the installed equipment base it says it supports.
news.limitations: FORT Robotics reported $12.5 million in revenue for the first nine months of 2026, up 52.5% year over year. Its proposed combination with Newbury Street II also brings disclosures about the installed base for robot-safety infrastructure. The registration form was filed on November 13 and discussed in the company's November 16 release. At publication it was not yet effective, with review and approvals for the combination still pending.
news.evidence_status: Company disclosure discussing registration documents; the proposed combination remains subject to approvals.
